passage: The cab had been stuck at the Silk Board junction for twenty minutes when a delivery rider cut in front of it, nearly scraping the door. Dilnaz threw up her hands. 'These delivery people are animals. No brains, no rules. They should all be banned from the roads.' Zeenat, who had to be at the airport by eight, took a breath. 'Remember Suresh? The one who brought our order in the flood last month?' 'That's one guy.' 'He told me he does fourteen hours a day to pay for his daughter's nursing college. And he gets fined if he's two minutes late.' Dilnaz was quiet. Outside, the rider who had cut in was checking his phone at the signal, a small boy's photo taped to his handlebar. 'Fine,' Dilnaz said. 'Not animals. Just...' 'Tired people on a timer,' Zeenat said. The signal changed.

qa.q: How many hours a day does Suresh work?
qa.a: Suresh does fourteen hours a day.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been thinking before taking a breath?
qa.a: Zeenat likely felt uneasy hearing a whole group called animals, and wanted to answer calmly with a real person rather than argue.

qa.q: Why was asking about Suresh more effective than arguing?
qa.a: Suresh's real story, the long hours, his daughter's college and the fines, gave the group a face, so Dilnaz's contempt softened into understanding without a fight.

qa.q: How might the rider at the signal see the traffic that evening?
qa.a: For the rider, with a child's photo on the handlebar and a timer running, the traffic is pressure to earn and avoid fines, not a game of breaking rules.

grounding: Shows an adult in a traffic jam who hears delivery riders called animals and answers with one real rider's life, bringing back empathy.

passage: At the housing society meeting in Thane, a resident stood up about the redevelopment. 'Once the chawl people move into Tower C, this place will become a slum. They're dirty, loud, no manners.' Heads nodded. Nikita, sitting near the back with her neighbour Tanuja, raised her hand. 'Can I ask about one person? Tanuja, didn't Lata-tai, who helps at your home, live in that chawl for thirty years?' Tanuja nodded and stood. 'Lata-tai raised three children there. Her son is a bank clerk now. She's the one who sat with my mother every afternoon when my mother was ill. She will be in Tower C.' The room shifted. The man who had spoken looked at his hands. Someone at the front said, 'Maybe we should invite the new families for the Ganpati function.' Nikita wrote it down in the minutes.

qa.q: How long did Lata-tai live in the chawl?
qa.a: Lata-tai lived in that chawl for thirty years.

qa.q: What might Nikita have felt as heads nodded around the room?
qa.a: Nikita likely felt uncomfortable watching a whole group dismissed as dirty, and wanted to bring one real face into the room.

qa.q: What made Nikita's question work?
qa.a: Asking about one person let Tanuja tell Lata-tai's true story, and the specific details moved the room from contempt to an invitation.

qa.q: How might Lata-tai feel if she knew about this meeting?
qa.a: Lata-tai might feel hurt by the first speaker's words but moved to be remembered for her kindness, and welcomed by the invitation.

grounding: Shows an adult at a society meeting who hears future neighbours called dirty and asks about one real person, bringing back empathy.

passage:
'Tarun, did you lock the scooter? Those labourers from the new site are all thieves,' Anand said, dropping his keys on the table.
'All of them?'
'Obviously. Look at them. Sitting on the footpath all evening.'
'Bhai, remember the one who fixed our water pump last week?'
'The thin fellow?'
'Raju. From Jharkhand. He wouldn't take extra money because it only took him ten minutes.'
'Okay, one honest one.'
'I asked him why they sit on the footpath. The contractor gives them one room for twelve men. They sit outside so the others can sleep.'
Anand was quiet. He picked up the keys again, turning them over.
'Twelve in one room?'
'Twelve.'
'Hm.' He went to the window. The men were there, one of them laughing on a video call. 'I didn't think about the room,' he said quietly.

qa.q: How many men share one room?
qa.a: Twelve men share one room.

qa.q: What does Anand turning the keys over suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Anand is unsettled, rethinking a quick judgement now that the men on the footpath have a reason and a face.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that brought back empathy?
qa.a: Tarun named one real person, Raju, and shared what Tarun had learned by asking him, which replaced 'all thieves' with a human story.

qa.q: What might the men on the footpath be feeling on these evenings?
qa.a: They may be tired and cramped, sitting outside so others can sleep, and a video call home might be the best part of the day.

grounding: Shows an adult who hears a brother call migrant workers thieves and answers with one man's name and real story.

passage:
I'm Ranjana. Last month at the team lunch, Gulnaz rolled her eyes about the new interns from the small-town colleges. 'Copy-paste machines. No brains, no English, just attendance.' People laughed. I almost did.
Instead I asked, 'Which one? Tell me about one of them.'
Gulnaz paused. 'Well... Mohit, the tall one.'
'What's Mohit like?'
'He comes in at eight because the bus from his village is the only one.' She stirred her dal. 'He asked me how to write a proper email. Twice.'
'Did he get it right the second time?'
She almost smiled. 'Better than some of us.'
The next week I saw her at Mohit's desk, going through his draft line by line. I think about that often. The whole group was easy to sneer at. One boy with a bus timetable wasn't.

qa.q: Why does Mohit come in at eight?
qa.a: Because the bus from his village is the only one.

qa.q: Why did Gulnaz's contempt seem to soften during the lunch?
qa.a: Talking about Mohit made her picture a real person who travels far and asked for help; she almost smiled, as if the sneer was harder to hold once she thought of him.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the lunch, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ranjana's question, 'Tell me about one of them', instead of laughing along; it moved Gulnaz from a sneer about a group to one person with a story.

qa.q: How might Mohit experience the change in Gulnaz the following week?
qa.a: Mohit now has a senior going through his draft line by line, which likely makes him feel noticed and helped rather than dismissed as a copy-paste machine.

grounding: An adult hears a group of interns described with contempt and asks about one of them, and the individual story brings back empathy.

passage:
Editor's note on trainee assessment. Ayesha, city desk.
Keerthana (24) sat in on Monday's meeting when the desk discussed the families near the canal who are being moved. A senior called them 'encroachers, the usual rent-seeking crowd', and the plan was a two-line brief.
Keerthana asked if she could spend a morning there first. She came back with Bhagyamma, a flower seller who has lived by the canal for nineteen years, whose grandson's school is next to it, and who keeps her voter card in a plastic bag against the rain.
Keerthana read her notes aloud at the evening meeting. The same senior asked, quietly, how far the new site was from the school.
We ran it as a full story with Bhagyamma's photo. I have asked Keerthana to lead the follow-up.

qa.q: How long has Bhagyamma lived by the canal?
qa.a: Bhagyamma has lived by the canal for nineteen years.

qa.q: What did Keerthana want when she asked to spend a morning at the canal first?
qa.a: She wanted to meet the real people behind the label before writing, sensing that 'encroachers' hid lives the desk had not seen.

qa.q: Which choice turned a two-line brief into a full story?
qa.a: Keerthana's choice to visit and listen to Bhagyamma, then read the notes aloud; one real face made the desk ask real questions, like how far the new site was from the school.

qa.q: What changed for the senior who used the word 'encroachers'?
qa.a: After hearing about Bhagyamma, the senior quietly asked how far the new site was from the school, a sign the contempt was giving way to concern for an actual family.

grounding: A young reporter hears a displaced group described with contempt, listens to one woman's story, and brings the desk's empathy back.
